Every birth is natural, and if it has to be a C-section, all the more respect to the mum, who will probably take longer to recover.
I had twins this year and twin 2 was transverse. I would have had no qualms with a C-section, but the operating theatre was engaged and so was the anaesthetist. So I had to go through 2 deliveries with no pain relief, 2 ECVs and 1 IPV (where the doctor inserts the hand in the uterus and pulls out the baby by the legs, a bit more with every contraction, and it feels like they’re trying to find the combination on a padlock). My babies and I were extremely lucky to have made it out unscathed, and we owe our lives and our health to the obstetrician. I’m 40 and I had 3 other deliveries before this, so I speak from experience. 
Yes, there are more C-sections. Mothers are older now and not as healthy or wealthy as their parents were when they had them. Women need to put off having kids because of low pay, lack of housing, and higher parenting standards. The days of latchkey kids are over. We’re expected to do more, spend more, and protect our kids better than our parents ever were. And I happen to think we’re doing a darn good job. I grew up in a time when kids were seen, not heard. I had no rights and my opinion was never sought. Any child with a disability was likely to be given up for adoption or institutionalised. The responsibilities and challenges of parenthood today are much, much greater. So, yes, perhaps mortality outcomes haven’t much changed even with C-sections. But if we want happy and healthy mums and babies, women have to be given access to immediate, high-quality medical care, including C-sections.
